speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
I have no objection. I think the motion of the hon. member for Simcoe (Mr. Currie) is now pretty clear, although I confess I did not understand it when I first read it. As I understand the explanation, certain questions as to the printing of the second report of the special committee mentioned were referred to the committee on printing, and they took the matter into consideration and made this recommendation. Paragraph 3 of this report would express the meaning intended to be conveyed, if after the word "recommendation" the words "for additional printing" were inserted. The same insertion should be made after the word "recommendation" in paragraph 4. The report of this committee deals altogether with the question of printing, which was properly referred to it in each case. However, the matter may stand until to-morrow.
Consideration of the third report of the Joint Committee on Printing deferred.

That the fourth report of the joint committee of both Houses on printing of Parliament be concurred in. He said: this report deals with the printing of Parliament and of the various departments. It contains suggestions, but makes no recommendations. A report was made last year, and a further report this year which is to be found on page 1094 of the Votes and Proceedings. For several years the committee have been endeavouring to bring about some reduction in the cost cf printing which has increased very greatly in recent years. It will be seen from this report that in 1913 the cost of the pri" ting of Parliament was $1,274,870. As a matter of fact, in five years it had increased from half a million to over a million and a quarter, and now in 1917 it is up to>
two and one-half millions dollars. We do not see that this expenditure is of any great importance, as far as information to the public is concerned. A report w.as made by the King's Printer with regard to the cost of printing of the various departments, which is referred to in this report. For instance, here is a report on the high cost of living. When that volume is completed and printed in French the cost to this country will be something like $40,000. That item was given me by the King's

Printer. Already $26,000 has been expended on the English edition, and, -with the French edition and the other two volumes, the total cost will be $40,000. That sum of money will uniform four battalions of infantry, or it -will provide four aeroplanes fully equipped. It will build four drill-halls, or four public post offices. Such unnecessary expenditures are being made annually, and there seems to be no one who can turn off the tap.
There is another report here on the Wabana iron mine which is in Newfoundland. The Mines Department, which is a great sinner in respect to additional increase in the cost of printing, has spent something like $5,000 publishing a big book with regard to a mine not in Canada, and with which Canada has nothing to do. There ie also a great deal published in regard to other matters which it would take a Philadelphia lawyer to understand. Volumes are published on the hydrometric survey of rivers away up on the Hudson bay which no one is interested in. This book is not only published once, but annually. This question of the cost of printing has been referred to us by this House to see if we can make some suggestion in regard to it. We have suggested that the map-making of the country should be placed! under one bureau, and that there should be standard maps. At present each department gets a fresh map, and there are hundreds and thousands of maps published which are of no use, whereas, if there were a standard map, reference could be made to it.
Then another matter for consideration is the material that is printed. We consider that the Government should take from the ranks of the Civil Service an editorial committee of, say, three men, to consider such questions and make suggestions. This editorial committee would meet and decide with regard to the publications in any department, and nothing but the personal order of the minister would override their decision. As near as I can ascertain, 80 per cent of the printing is done without reference to the ministers of the different departments. If there were an editorial board of that kind, the various departmental officers, if they wanted to publish anything in regard to the Wabana iron mine would make a report, which would come before the minister, giving an estimate of the cost, and the minister would consider whether it would be in the interest of the country to spend ten or fifteen thousand dollars in useless work. That committee would also prevent duplication. We have been endeavouring to prevent duplication in the various departments. Some of the -most expensive documents issued by the Government are those dealing with trade, and we are endeavouring to arrange so that there will be only one publication dealing with trade, whereas at present there are two or three. The Census Branch issues a publication dealing with the trade question, and t'he Customs Department publishes two or three volumes dealing with other such matters, and the Department of Trade and Commerce issues other publications. This matter has been going on previous to this Government coming into power, nothing has been initiated by this Government to create additional cost. We *think there should be something done to improve the system and that this proposed board should have the supervision of these matters, and refer to the chief of the department any publication in that department that they did not consider it advisable to print. The report is before the committee. There is no recommendation that requires an expenditure of money.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
The effective suggestion which has been placed before the House by the committee is this:
The most effective way to bring about economies in Canadian Parliamentary and Departmental printing is, in the opinion of the committee, to create an editorial board of three members of the Civil Service, thoroughly conversant with public affairs, and with a knowledge of Departmental workings. This board should have plenary powers' to order such excisions of "copy" of Departmental reports, leaflets, bulletins, memoirs, etc., or to refuse to sanction the printing of any report if, in their judgment, the public interest would not be seriously affected by such refusal.
It would be the duty of the Board to call upon the Deputy Head of any Department or Branch of the Public Service created by Parliament, whose requisition and "copy" for printing were under consideration, to show cause why any proposed reductions in "copy" should not be made or, the printing thereof suspended entirely, and only upon direct written authority of the Minister of the Department interested [DOT] should the decision of the Board of Editors be countermanded.
The Board should present a report of its operations annually to Parliament within three weeks after the opening of each session thereof, such report to give the dates when first and last "copy" of every departmental report is received, and specifying the reductions in text, and the reasons therefor. In cases where the decision of the Board has been overridden by the Minister of any department Parliament shall be advised.
The suggestions1 in the three paragraphs which I have just read are worthy of at-

tentive consideration; that consideration will be given. I have already discussed the subject to some extent with my colleagues, and I feel confident that we shall either adopt the report of the committee as it has been presented to the House, or modify it to the extent of (having two or three members of the Government associated with the members of the Civil Service in the editorial committee referred to. That might, perhaps be desirable. However, we have not reached a fixed conclusion on that point. I am confident that some effective way of carrying out the suggestions of the committee will be found.
It is pointed out- in the report that in some of the departments the recommendations made last year by the committee have been pretty fully carried out. In other departments, it is thought, there is still room for improvement. This report will be commended to the consideration of the permanent 'head of each department with a view to having the suggestions of the committee carried out in their entirety in the respective departments, unless there is good reason to the contrary. It is possible that in making some of these comments the committee did not have before them absolutely full information as to the subjects which are dealt with, but generally speaking I believe that the suggestions are worthy of consideration, which will be accorded.
As to the increased cost of printing during the last five years, it is due in part to the increased printings rendered necessary by the war and in part to the increased cost of paper, which has been very great, especially during the past two years. I have no objection to the House concurring in the report which the committee have made.

I am not sure that I approve the recommendations made with regard to certain information which is annually given to Parliament. The information given to Parliament by any department is under the responsibility of the minister; he prepares his own report every, year, and he may supplement that report by other information which he thinks it advantageous to publish. I do not think that we can gain anything by taking away the responsibility of the minister in this matter. I see here that several-I will not say criticisms, rather reflections, are made with respect to some of the publications. The report of the committee says:
"Economy" will have to be Canada's watchword tor many years to come, and the printing:

Bills of Parliament and the public Departments present a fertile field for action in this regard. That our great neighbours to the south realize this in connection with Congressional publications is shown by the decision of the Senate of the United States to cut down this year its printing hills by $470,080. This has been brought about by reducing the bulk of some reports and suspending entirely the publication of others.
Well, that is a matter for the minister. He is giving the information to f>he public; it is for him to see that that information is as concise as possible. It does not follow that the giving of the information should be entirely suppressed. Then the report goes on to mention the United States reports which have been cut down:
Among the latter may be mentioned: Monthly Summary of Foreign Commerce, Annual Report of Foreign Commerce and Navigation, Report of District of Columbia Health Office, Bulletins of the Bureau of Ethnology, annual report ditto; Bulletins of the Bureau of Fish -eries. Geological Bulletins, Geological Professional papers, Geological Water Supply papers, Memoirs of the National Academy of Sciences, Nautical Almanac, Annual Report of Bureau of Soils, and many others.
Some of our publications are similar to these. The Department of Trade and Commerce issues a good many reports; according to this recommenda/tion, the precedent of the United States should be followed and many of those reports should he cut down. The report oi the committee says that in the United States the monthly summary of foreign commerce has been eliminated. We have something like that here; it is a very useful publication, and should not be cut down. We have also a report of foreign commerce and navigation; I would say the same about that report. If we find that departmental publications are too bulky or give useless information, we can call attention to the matter, but for my part I should not like to suppress the publication of these reports or to take away from the minister the responsibility of having them brought down in proper form.

It is not the intention of the committee to take any of the responsibility from the minister. The formation of an editorial board will not have that effect; it will not interfere with the duties of the minister or the functions of the departments. It will endeavour to cut down the size of the volume by better editorial work and it will point out to a minister, when any of his officials send in a volume for publication, whether any other department has published a similar volume. The Conservation Commission, for instance, is issu-

mg very extensive reports covering matters that have already been covered by other departments. The editorial board would have supervision in that regard. The committee had no intention of interfering with the duties of any of the ministers or the work of any of the departments; the only desire was to see that more supervision should be exercised with a view to preventing too great a cost in the publication of these reports. The Auditor 'General's _ Report, for instance, has been published in English and in French. The department has decided to publisn the headings in English and in French and to put the whole thing m one volume. For years we have been spending about $25,000 more than was necessary on that report. The intention of the committee was, according to the request of Parliament, to bring in a report with a view to a reduction in the cost of printing. We are at war, and it is necessary for us to economize. On behalf of the committee, I thank the Prime Minister for his suggestion that the departments should be asked to give consideration to the report.
Motion agreed to, and fourth report of the committee concurred in.
That the fifth report of the joint committee of both Houses on the printing of Parliament be concurred in.

On the Orders o.f the Day:

At the front, officers, non-commissioned officers and men of the various divisions are, by authority, allowed to wear distinctive badges. Soldiers from those divisions returning to Canada have (been in the habit of wearing them. Recently, by somebody's order, not always carried out in the most courteous manner, officers, non-commissioned officers and men, on reaching Canada, have been brusquely told to remove .those badges. I would ask the Minister of Militia by whose authority that is done and why?

The badges to which my hon. friend refers are what are known as identification (badges of the divisions at the front. The badge appears on the arm or sometimes on the back of the tunic. They are no.t badges for distinguished conduct in the war. I understand the badges for the Victoria Cross and the Distinguished Service Order are not on all fours with these badges. The order is an order of the Imperial Army, and requires those badges to be removed when the soldiers leave France if they are on leave. I have only heard of one case in this country in which a soldier has been spoken to on the street, and there was no attempt at that time to speak to the soldiers in a discourteous manner. It was the provost-marshal who spoke to the man about his wearing the badge being against the regulations.
I have twenty instances, and I want to know why soldiers are not permitted to wear those badges in Canada.
It is an order of the Imperial Army, and the Canadian Army follows that order in that soldiers remove those badges when they leave France.
I have never seen such an order for the Imperial service, although I have tried verj hard to find it. I have known officers returned to England being ordered to wear those badges.
On the Orders of the Day:

I would ask the Minister of Militia if an order has been promulgated permitting soldiers of the First Division to wear their blue shoulder strap? There is an Imperial order in England to that effect. I understand that some provosLmarshals have ordered soldiers to take off their blue shoulder badge or, if they are in the artillery, their red shoulder badge.
I am unable to answer my hon. friend's question to-day. I will endeavour to obtain information regarding it.
Bill No. 132, to amend the Companies Act. -Mr. Meighen.
The House proceeded to the consideration of an amendment made by the Senate to Bill No. 66, to amend the Judges Act.-Mr. Doherty.

speakeroldname: Hon. C. J. DOHERTY (Minister of Justice) :
speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
This Bill, as introduced into this House, provided simply salaries for an additional High Court judge of the province of Saskatchewan, as required by the legislation of that province, and for a County Court judge in the province of Ontario similarly required, and it made a regulation as to the travelling expenses of judges and as to the application to circuit court judges in Montreal of the provinces providing for inquiries applicable to the present County Court judges.
The Bill as it left this House was approved by the Senate in its entirety, but that honourable body added a number of amendments dealing with the general subject of the duties of judges. I am not prepared to say that certain of those amendments in principle might not be accepted, but before we could accept them I think they would require considerable modification from the very general terms in which they are expressed, and the very general effect given to them. They raise a very important question which it seems to me can hardly be dealt with suitably by this House in considering amendments introduced by the other House to a Bill of this nature, and especially at this .stage of the session, when it is difficult, if not impossible, to give to these important amendments the consideration they deserve.
The first of these proposed amendments is to repeal certain legislation enacted in the year 1906. That legislation, which amended previously existing legislation, made special provision for the payment of full pensions to judges after they had reached a certain age and had served a certain number of years upon the bench. The amendment before us proposes to repeal the legislation of 1906, which would leave the law as it stood previously to that time, and provide for the pryment of a two-thirds pension only, in cases where a man had served fifteen years or had become incapacitated by illness. Speaking for myself, I would raise no objection to the proposed repeal, but for the fact that it raises an important question as to the protection and preservation of the rights of judges appointed under that legislation. The only proviso in the amendment protecting any vested right is one .to protect the rights of judges who have actually
[Sir Edward Kemp.l
retired under that law and are in receipt of tiieir pensions.
The next amendment deals with section 33 of the Judges Act, ighich in general terms prohibits judges from engaging in any other occupation or business. The proposed amendment would prohibit the judges from performing any duties outside of their judicial duties. I am not prepared to say that there would not be an advantage in making more precise the prohibitions at present existing, but the prohibition as adopted by the Senate is very widely beyond the mark, because it is obvious that there are some duties that man must perform, even though he be a judge, which are not judicial duties.
The other amendments follow, I think, upon this last-mentioned' one. They contain a prohibition against the judge receiving a remuneration for the performance of any duty outside of his judicial duties. As the section stands, he is already prohibited from performing any such duty, and the amendment makes certain limitations and restrictions to the general prohibition proposed, in favour of duties imposed by the provincial legislatures.
I am not prepared to say that in principle these amendments have not a great deal to commend them to the consideration of this House, but it seems to me quite clear that before we could accept them they would have to be modified in very important particulars in their wording. As I have already said, they bring up very important questions in connection with the independence of the judiciary, which I think deserve very careful consideration before such serious modifications in the law are made.
Although I have had no formal conference,
I have had some communication with the hon. gentlemen of the Senate and they seem disposed rather to share the view that these important questions could be dealt with in another manner. For these reasons, I beg to move:
That the amendments made by the Senate to this Bill be not concurred in, and that a message to that effect be sent to that honourable House.

Please read
the amendments one by one.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: I must present the motion as I have it, unless the minister consents to alter it.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: There is no objection on my part if it is thought desirable, but the same reasons apply to all the amendments.
What is the nature of these amendments?

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext:
The amendment is:
Page 1, line 32.-After clause 4 add clauses 5, 6, 7, 8 and 9, as follows:
5. (1) Sections 20, 22, as enacted by section 3 of chapter 39 of the statutes of 1908, and 26, as enacted by section 9 of chapter 28 of the statutes of 1913, of the said Act are hereby repealed; but such repeal shall not be construed to affect the pension of any judge who before the passing of this Act has resigned or been retired.
(2) Section 26 of the said Act, as enacted by section 9 of chapter 28 of the statutes of 1913, is amended by striking out the words "sections 24 and 25" and substituting therefor the words "section 24."

Why is section 25 left out? As I understand the amendment, it limits the pension !a judge of a Superior Court shall receive after a certain length of service, or after he has reached a certain age, to two-thirds of his salary, but it leaves the law as at present, regarding the right of a judge to retire after a shorter period in case of illness.
I am inclined to think there is a great deal of good sense in the amendment which has been made by the Senate. If the country provides that after a reasonable term of service a judge may retire with two-thirds of his salary, and enjoy the leisure a judge is no doubt entitled to enjoy -upon retirement, the country would be treating him with a fair measure of justice, and I, for one, would be disposed to support the amendment which has been made by the Senate.

I agree with my
hon. friend from St. John (Mr. Pugsley). There are instances throughout the country where judges have reached the age when it is known to the Bar they are not able to give that full service to the country which ought to be expected from them, but they carry on a little longer than they otherwise would with the hope of getting their full salary on retirement. One does not need to particularize these cases, because I am quite Isure hon. gentlemen know of them. This is not a desirable state of affairs. It is a good rule and in the interests of the country, and would be more satisfactory in the administration of justice, that judges should retire after the period of service fixed by the Act, with the certainty of getting two-thirds of their salaries, and that they should not get any more by prolonging their stay upon the Bench. I do not very well see why the Minister of Justice would not accept an amendment of that kind.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: The amendment which it is now sought to strike out of the Judges Act was introduced, I think, in 1908, and there was a subsequent amendment in 1913. The considerations upon which that legislation was submitted to Parliament were very mulch along the line just placed before the House by my hon. friend from St. John and my hon. friend from Pictou (Mr. Macdonald). It was supposed that the operation of the Act in question would bring about the retirement of judges after a certain period, and under conditions when that retirement might be considered to be in the public interest; that is to say, it was believed at that time, whether rightly or wrongly, that a judge sometimes continued in the discharge of his judicial duties for a longer period than was consistent with the public interest because of his desire to retain his full salary by continuing in office, which desire, from his standpoint, might have been emphasized by the condition of his personal affairs. Then it was supposed that if a judge had given a certain service, or reached a certain age, and if he was in a position to retire upon his full salary, a condition then thought undesirable would he remedied, and the very thing which my hon. friends desire to avoid would be avoided. I am not at all confident that the operation of the statute has been precisely along the lines anticipated when th:.-4 p.m. legislation was first introduced, and I believe there is good reason for reconsidering it. At the same time, 1 do not think it can be reconsidered in precisely the form which has been suggested, nor do I think it desirable that we should undertake the revision of the Act by the method which is suggested here, namely, an amendment to a Bill of this character. We must remember that one of the most important principles with regard to the independence of judges-and no one could overrate the importance of that consideration-is permanence of tenure of office during good behaviour, and fixity of remuneration. It is therefore apparent that continued or repeated changing of the salaries of judges, or of the pensions to which they become entitled upon their retirement, is undesirable. For that reason also, I think it important that the principle of the amendment and the method of the amendment should be very carefully considered, and that it would hardly do for this House, with the hurried consideration we can give the matter at present, to deal with so important a subject now.

I do not rise to a point of order, but so far as my experience goes, when a Bill comes amended from the Senate, the question is first put upon one amendment, then upon the second, then upon the third, because the House may concur in one, and not in another.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: I will look up the point. As I view it at present, I think it is open for the House to concur in or reject the amendments as a whole. In any event, the motion is in respect of the first amendment.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
I think my right hen. friend is perfectly correct, as a matter of procedure. We are proceeding with the amendments one by one. There are five different sections added to the Bill, and we are taking them one after another. L think the matter had better be postponed, for another reason. When we do not concur in an amendment made by the Senate to one of our Bills, it is usual that we should accompany the non-concurrence with the reasons. My hon. friend (Mr. Doherty) has stated the reasons in his observations, bu:. it seems to me, practice requires that they should be more formally stated, and should be embodied in the motion presented to the House. I would therefore suggest, Mr. Speaker, that the matter be taken up on another day, when the motion would embody the reasons which would lead the House to the conclusion that the amendments be not concurred in. What I say would apply to the section as to which we have already expressed	non-concurrence-that is it
should be regarded as still open, for the purpose I have mentioned.

I move that the debate be now adjourned.
Motion agreed to and debate adjourned.

I sincerely hope that Bill will pass the Senate, although there is isome controversy about certain clauses. If that Bill should not be passed

by the Senate, it is desirable that the measure before U6 should b.e passed by this House, and for that reason I desire to take it up to-day.
Motion, agreed to.
On motion of Sir Robert Borden Bill 103 concerning the salaries or wages of employees of railway companies, was read the second time, and the House went into committee thereon, Mr. Rainville in the Chair.
On section 1-R.S., c. 37; a. 259 amended. Payment of wages.

This Bill 6eems to be an exact counterpart of a section which we added to the Consolidated Railway Act, which provides that the employee shall be paid semi-monthly. I am heartily in sympathy with the provision.

speechtext: In case the Railway Bill should not pass the Senate, I think it is desirable this legislation should be enacted, but I shall not move the third reading of it at present, in the hope that the Railway Bill will pass the Senate, because it would be undesirable to have the same enactment in two different Bills.

I feel that it would be a great misfortune if the Consolidated Railway Bill did not get through the Senate, especially as I understand there is no question about the provisions of that Bill, excepting two matters, which are very largely-I was going to say-personal and local affairs. One of these matters is some sort of a quarrel between the Hydro-Electric in Ontario, and the Toronto Electric Light Ci mpany and the Toronto and Niagara Power Company. The other difference is between the Bell Telephone Company and the Independent Telephone Companies. The special railway committee occupied six or seven weeks in considering this measure, and representatives of labour unions and other interests in Canada attended the meetings of this committee and took part in the discussion, and I think it would be a great misfortune if all the time and labour of the special railway committee and of these gentlemen representing other interests should go for naught, and that the Bill should not become law. I simply opposed these clauses as a matter of principle and had no personal interest, but if it should turn out that these two clauses were the only hitch, surely they will drop them and hu us have the Bill, because I think there were very many important changes embodied in that measure which the business of this
country demands. Nothing has happened in my somewhat lengthy Parliamentary career that has pleased me any more than the sense of public duty which seemed to inspire the special 'Committee of this House which considered that Bill. There were no politics in it. I never saw an instance, from the beginning to the end, where political feeling played the faintest part in the consideration of the measure. Every one was actuated by the desire to make that Bill as perfect and workable as possible, and the underlying principle of the whole Bill was that wherever there was a question of dispute between corporations and the public, it was invariably left to the Railway Board to decide, and while I do not know that they want any bouquets or compliments from me, I may say that I think the Railway Board to-day is an institution of which this country should be proud. I feel that we are safe in leaving disputed matters to a board of that kind, and, therefore, if the Senate cannot agree on those two clauses, I hope an arrangement will be made by which the remainder of the Bill will become law, and those two matters can be taken up next session.

It is beyond question that the members of the board are inspired by a strong sense of public duty, and give the best of their energy and ability to the work with which they are charged. It would be a great pity if the work of the special committee, which reported the Railway Bill to the House, should be lost. I am very glad to hear what my hon. friend has said of the work of that committee. It is entirely in accordance with what I have heard from other sources. It is most desirable that the Bill should be passed. I can assure my hon. friend that I have impressed that point as strongly as is in my power upon those now dealing with the Bill. It is my hope that it may get through. If it should not pass, it is important that this provision, and possibly one or two other provisions which were inserted in the Railway Bill, should become <*. I do not think any explanation of the provisions of the Bill before us is required. It is a very simple Bill.

speechtext:
I take advantage of this -motion, Mr. Speaker, to bring to the attention of the House a matter of very great importance. I should have brought the matter up earlier in the session had it not been for the fact that upon previous occasions when the House was going into -Committee of Supply I was unable to arrange with the Minister of Marine and Fisheries (Hon. J. D. Hazen) for a discussion of the matter upon days convenient either to ihim ox to myself. In this respect I do not blame the minister, whose department the matter specially affects. He spoke to me last week expressing his desire that the -question should be discussed, and regretting that personal reasons compelled him to leave here on Saturday.
The matter which I desire to bring to the attention of the House is the right of the Victoria Sealing Company, of British Columbia, composing nine-tenths of the people engaged in the sealing industry in Canada, to participate in the fund which is to-day in the hands of the Government as a result of the Pelagic Sealing Treaty which was entered into at Washington, on July 7, 1911. In order that the House may fully understand the matter, it will be necessary for me to read from public documents at .some length, but in a comprehensive way I shall state at the beginning the facts of the case.
On the date which I have mentioned there was a gathering at Washington of representatives of the United States, Russia, Japan, and Canada-the latter acting on behalf of Great Britain-and there was entered into what is known as the Pelagic Sealing Treaty. Under that treaty, in consideration of British subjects giving up the right to sealing in the Pacific ocean, Canada was- to receive a certain percentage of the value of the seal skins taken by the United States, Russia, and Japan at their respective rookeries in the Northern Pacific. The treaty was for a period of fifteen years from December 15, 1911, or so long there-

after as the treaty should not be terminated by either one of the contracting parties giving twelve months' notice of their desire to bring it to a conclusion. For the period of fifteen years British subjects refrained from engaging in pelagic sealing, and there will be paid to Canada in respect of that period an amount approximating $-7,250,000. Already $200,000 have been paid by the United States to Canada on account of the amount payable to Canada as a compensation for her refraining from engaging in the sealing industry. There existed in British Columbia at that time what was known as the Victoria -Sealing Company, which had been formed in the year 1900 by British Columbia sealers, all British subjects engaged in the sealing industry. This company controlled 43 out of the 46 vessels on the Pacific coast engaged in the sealing industry.
The money received by the Government of Canada under the treaty mentioned was not to go into the treasury, but to compensate those who had been engaged in the industry, and who, by reason of Canada's undertaking, were prevented from further engaging in this very profitable means of earning money and of developing an industry. Out of that $200,000 there has been paid out, as the result of certain recommendations made by Mr. Justice Audette, the sum of $60,000; the balance is in the hands of the Government. That amount of approximately $60,000 was not paid to the company to which I have referred; they claim that it should have been paid to them. Under the facts which I propose to present, I submit that this Government should provide for the payment of that money to the Victoria Sealing Company. Not only should the remainder of the amount received be paid over to them, but also whatever amount should be arrived at, upon a proper assessment of damages based upon those considerations, not purely of law, but of equity and fair dealing, which, according to our legal authorities, bind the Government in their dealings with subjects in cases of this kind.
The complaint is that the Government retain that money, and apparently propose to retain future moneys paid in on that account, without any regard to these owners of 43 vessels which had been engaged in the sealing industry. I wi-sh to press upon the Government the wisdom of providing for an .assessment of damages. Had we been able to bring the matter to the attention of the House at an earlier date, which unfortunately we were not for the reasons

I have 'mentioned, we should have asked the Government to provide that the matter he left to a committee of the House for investigation. Or, if that were not done, a tribunal might be constituted to assess the damages on the basis I have stated.
That the House may be properly seized of the facts, I may be permitted to give some general information upon the subject. By a Treaty between Her late Majesty's Government and the Government of the United States, an agreement was come to whereby the matters in dispute between the two powers relating to the Behring sea fisheries were submitted to a tribunal which met at Paris in 1893. On that tribunal Great Britain was represented by the late Lord Hannen and the late Sir John Thompson, then Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada; the late Sir Charles Russell, former English Attorney General, and afterwards Lord Chief Justice of England, and Sir Charles Hibbert Tupper, who at that time was Minister of Marine and Fisheries of the Canadian Government, weie counsel for the British Government. The claim put forward on behalf of the United States at that time was to the effect that the Behring sea was a "mare clausum," or closed sea, and that, therefore, the British sealers had no right to fish there. Having regard to the principles of maritime law which applied to different nations as to seas which were known as closed seas within the terms of international law, power was given to the Paris tribunal to decide the question, and it was also agreed, in the event of their denying the claim of the United States, that they should make such regulations as they might deem advisable for the preservation and protection of the Behring sea seal fisheries.
The events which led up to the arbitration are: The sealing industry of British Columbia began in 1873 by the fitting out of a few vessels for hunting seals in the North Pacific ocean and the Behring sea. It gradually grew in importance until, at the time of the Paris arbitration, there were 59 sealing vessels sailing out of the port of Victoria, and the industry supplied occupation and profit to some 1,500 people. During the period above-mentioned, the only other people who engaged in seal fishing in the Behring sea to any extent were subjects of the United States. There was, however, a considerable difference in the manner of killing the seals as between British subjects and the citizens of the United
States. I do not want to go into the details of pelagic sealing, but it is necessary for the purpose o<f understanding the matter to know that the teals have their "rookeries" on shore, to which they resort for breeding purposes, and none of these rookeries are situate in British territory, but are situate in the territories of the United States, Japan and Russia. The British sealers, therefore, were obliged to pursue their industry entirely on the high seas, whereas the American sealers did most of their killing on land, the privilege o.f doing which the United States Government leased to certain of its citizens, just as we give canning licenses to men who engage in the lobster industry or fishing licenses to those who engage in that industry. In the year 1886 armed revenue cutters of the United States began to seize all British sealers operating in the Behring sea, and the British sealers appealing for protection, their right to pursue their calling on the high seas was supported by the British Government. Diplomatic negotiations took place with the United States Government, and in the year 1891 a temporary modus vivendi was arrived at whereby a partial and temporary prohibition of sealing on the high seas was agreed to, somewhat similar to the permanent prohibition which was finally determined by the arrangement at Washington in 1911. At that time the position taken by Great Britain was expressed by the Right Hon. W. H. Smith, then the leader of the British House of Commons, who, in announcing to the House the arrangement arrived at, said:
I am going to do a friendly act in the interests of a friendly power, but if I do that and interfere with certain men and their business, I shall pay compensation out of the British Exchequer, upon proof being made to the commissioner as to how far they have been affected by that partial prohibition.
At that period of our history in connection with this question, the British Government laid down the proposition that the parties who had been engaged in this industry, the continuance of which was interfered with by arrangements with a foreign power, should, in equity and right, receive compensation by reason of the fact that they were debarred for the time being from pursuing their lawful occupation. The result was that following the policy announced by Mr. Smith, the sum of $200,000 was paid out of the British Exchequer to the Victoria sealers as compensation for the partial and temporary prohibition which involved

speechtext:
July 7, 1911. It will be noted that that report of Mr. Found was made practically at the time of entering into the treaty, and therefore is of more significance, because those were the conditions under which the treaty was entered into, with the full knowledge and belief that these gentlemen composing the company were going to get compensation. A specific recommendation which, he made in regard to that reads:
Article 11 of the Treaty provides for an advance payment by the United States to Great Britain of $200,000 on account of seal skins to which Great Britain is entitled under the Treaty. This money has already been paid over to Canada and can he made available by authority of your Royal Highness for the payment of compensation to those damnified by the Treaty. No doubt the object in securing such advanced payment was to enable the necessary compensation to he paid without drawing on the treasury.
In the opinion of the undersigned, in the light of the conditions obtaining such sum will provide liberal compensation to those directly affected by the Treaty and should not therefore be exceeded.
The undersigned has therefore the honour to recommend:
(1) That compensation be paid out of the $200,000 received from the United States government under the Treaty and that the total amount paid in such connection do not exceed that sum.

He varies that recommendation by a more liberal interpretation in another part of the report, which I will not read to the House. I am quoting from Mr. Found's statement in regard to the matter, because it proves conclusively that the Government officials in Canada, who had everything to do with the question of working out this treaty arrangement, recognize unequivocally, as between man and man, according to the principles of morality, equity, and justice as administered by a court of law, that the Victoria Sealing Company were entitled, upon that basis, to receive compensation. There can be no manner of doubt about that.
Now, Mr. Justice Audette acting as a commissioner, finally made a report on this matter, after long delay, on the 10th day of January, 1916. It is complained on behalf of the sealing company, and on behalf of Sir Hibbert Tupper, that the first knowledge he received of the finding of Mr. Justice Audette or his opinion rather, was some statement in a fishing magazine, at any rate, it was not until the summer of last year that they were able to get the document printed in answer to a return in this House. He deals with the various classes of eases that were submitted to him. He divides that classification.submitted to him into four. Therefore, it may be stated that he disposes of the sum of $60,000 out of $200 000, but he declines to give any sum to the sealing company as compensation, notwithstanding the facts I have mentioned m detail to the House in regard to the whole question. He says:
Having- thus passed in review the general heads of complaint put forward by the sealers against the regulations, and approaching the consideration of this claim in a spirit of justice connoting the idea of doing what in equity and good conscience is fair and just, and after giving this branch of the commission special care and labour, as it involved both large amounts and a large number of claimants, I have come to the conclusion and find that the Canadian sealers are not entitled to be paid any compensation by the Crown for alleged damage resulting from the said regulations.
Of course, his opinion is nothing more than a,n opinion, because no jurisdiction, authority, or power, was conferred upon Judge Audette to make any final decision in the matter. It is in accordance with that opinion, which was afterwards affirmed by an Order in Council made by the Government last year, that I appeal to the Gov^ eminent and this House to look into this matter, and deal with it upon the broadest principles, and upon the most generous lines.

It seems to me that one cannot look over these facts presented here and say that the Government can be doing their full duty if they disregard the fact that this money came into their hands simply as trustees for Canadian citizens.
It is not the money of the Government of Canada; the Government holds it in trust for those who were entitled to compensation and who were damnified in any way by the operation of these regulations.
The learned judge based his con elusion that the Victoria Sealing Company was not entitled to compensation upon several grounds. First, he said that the provisions of the Paris regulations were analogous to any other restrictions imposed upon an industry by a State for the benefit of all those engaged in the industry. He says in effect that the men engaged in the sealing industry have no more right to complain of the Paris regulations than men engaged in the salmon or lobster industry have a right to complain about a change made in the fishing season. I submit that that is very narrow ground to take on an international question. To say that matters affecting the . interests of people engaged in this international industry should he settled on the same basis as matters affecting people engaged in am industry such as lobster fishing, which is carried on only during certain months of the year, is hardly taking broad grounds. I do not think that Sir John Thompson, Lord Justice Hannen, Sir Charles Russell and Sir Charles Hibbert Tupper, when they sat in Paris and promulgated these regulations, were looking at this matter from that viewpoint. Matters affecting those engaged in this international industry ought to be settled on the same high plane -as that taken by the plenipotentiaries of the great powers who met first in Paris and afterwards in Washington.
The learned judge stated as a second reason, for his. conclusion that the Paris regulations did not provide for any compensation to the sealers. This was primarily the reason why the Canadian Government insisted at the 1911 conference at Washington that the compensation should be given.
It was because these Paris regulations provided for no compensation that Sir John Thompson objected to their being put in operation. The Government of the day, as shown in the letter that I read from the then Prime Minister, Sir Joseph Pope, pointed out that no arrangement could be made except on the basis of compensation. These

Paris regulations were passed in the interests of the United States sealing people. When in 1911 the matter was being dealt with, it was suggested that, the industry having suffered on account of these regulations, some compensation should be provided.
The learned' judge, in his opinion, said further that the sealers had no legal rights that could be enforced against the Crown. That, of course, is a legal truism. But the relation between Sovereign and subject is put very clearly in the illuminating judgments given in England in a case having relation to a treaty under which money was to be similarly disposed of. The judgments are those of Chief Justice Cockburn and Mr. Justice Lush in the well-known case of Rustomjee vs. the Queen in the Exchequer Court of England, and, on appeal, of Lord Chief Justice Coleridge. Chief Justice C'ockburn said:
The effect of the .	.	. treaty-
He is referring not to the Pelagic Sealing Treaty, hut to another.
-is .	.	. simply this, that it places the
fund at the disposition of Her Majesty for Her Majesty at her discretion to cause distribution of it to be made as shall make good the claims which her subjects have against the foreigner from whose Government the money is received.
Mr. Justice Lush said:
No doubt a duty arose as soon as the money was received to distribute that money amongst the persons towards whose losses it was paid .	.	.	; the distribution when made would he
the act of a sovereign in dispensing justice to her subjects. .	. For any omission of that
duty the sovereign cannot be held responsible. The responsibility would rest with the advisers of the Crown, and they are responsible to Parliament and to Parliament alone.
And lastly on appeal, Lord Chief Justice Coleridge said:
We do not doubt that on the payment of the money .	.	. there was a duty on the part
of the English Sovereign to administer the money so received according to the stipulations of the treaty. But it was a duty to do justice to her subjects according to the advice of her responsible ministers.
These are the principles upon which funds of this kind were disposed of, according to English decision; and these are the principles which should guide the Canadian Government in dealing with 'this question. I again assert that the money w-hich the Government have received and which they will receive from time to time during the next fifteen years is not the property of the Government of Canada per se; it is in
their possession as trustees along the line of the decisions to which I have referred.
It must be borne in mind that if it had not been for the Victoria Sealing Company, the Canadian Government would have had no claim to compensation. Besides those owned by the company, only four vessels, operated by Japanese and Indians, were engaged in the sealing industry in British Columbia, in defiance of the regulations. I have pointed out that in 1911 the 35 vessels of the company were tied up at the wharf, prevented from sealing on account of these regulations. Had it not been for that fact, the Government of Great Britain would have had no case for compensation in the negotiations at Washington, because there would have been nobody to compensate.
With regard to the opinion of Mr. Justice Audette, I wish to read a telegram *sent by Sir Charles Hibbert Tupper to the Minister of Marine and Fisheries from Vancouver'on May 20, 1913. It is as follows :
Telegraphic report of Commission re sealers in effect bars out all claims save those affected by treaty 1911. Kindly wire if scope not intended to include the claims of those affected by regulations under Behring Sea Award.
To which the minister replied, on May 21, 1913:
Telegraphic report incorrect. Commission will enquire into validity of claims under Behring Sea Award and report to Government as to whether or not such claims should be entertained.
So that it was the intention of- the commission to consider these claims and to have a report upon them. Then there is various correspondence in which Sir Charles Hibbert Tupper as counsel for the sealers complains that he was not advised as to the filing of the report; that not until it had been brought down in the House last year, during the midsummer, and finally printed had he received a copy.
On February 28, 1916 an Order in Council was passed- approving of the opinion given by Mr. Justice Audette. Sir Charles Hibbert Tupper came to Ottawa and on November 1, 1916 he advised the Victoria Sealing Company as follows: "
During my visit in Ottawa I had a conversation with the Prime Minister and all I can say is that he seemed favourably disposed, so far as he was personally concerned, to allow a rehearing, but felt it would be necessary to convince the Minister of Marine that the sealers' request be complied with. I think I have already told you the idea the Minister of Marine entertained, viz.: that Audette made an award or a judgment and that this was final.
I think I successfully pointed out to the Prime Minister that this was not a proper view; that by the Order in Council and Com-

mission Audette was appointed a commissioner to take evidence and if he saw fit, to report with the evidence his opinion.
It would be unfortunate, in a case of this kind, if the Government or the Minister of Marine and Fisheries undertook to hold that Mr. Justice Audette's report on this matter was in the nature of a judgment which was final. It can be readily seen, from the Order in Council which I read and from the commission issued to Mr. Justice Audette, that it was not intended that he should dispose of the matter in the same way as a court would dispose of it, and in the second place, it would be most unfair to those gentlemen who had created a case for the Government in this international matter which had formed the subject of consideration at Paris and Washington, if they were to be told here: There is no appeal from this inquiry; we, the trustees for this money, will not listen to a request from you to be classed as a cestui que trust; we have created a tribunal, and although your claims are based upon the broadest grounds of justice, equity and fair play, yet, we will not consider those matters upon that basis, and we will simply hang upon the decision of Mr. Justice Audette upon the point, and let the matter stand.
The result was that on the 21st of November, 1916, Mr. Adams of the Victoria Sealing Company wrote to the Minister of Marine and Fisheries, as follows:
On the 26th of April last the Victoria Sealing Company, Ltd., sent you a protest against the findings of Mr. Justice Audette regarding the Sealing Commission, for which he was appointed commissioner. A reply to the petition that a rehearing of the matter be given has never been received by this company, although the shareholders have been anxiously looking for it all this time. Would you kindly let us know whether the petition for a rehearing is to be granted, or whether it is refused.
To this letter the deputy Minister of the Naval Service replied on November 29:
I beg to acknowledge your letter of the 22nd ultimo, calling attention to the protest of the Victoria Sealing Company, Limited, against the findings of Mr. Justice Audette in connection with the Pelagic sealing claims, and the request for a hearing in the way of appeal before the Governor in Council or otherwise.
In reply, I am directed to state that as the claimants were given full opportunity to substantiate their claims before the commissioner, and the award was made in the light of the evidence submitted, it has been decided after careful consideration of the matter, to accept the award of Mr. Justice Audette as a final closing of the case.
Then there is this letter written on December 16 by the Victoria Sealing Com-

pany to the deputy Minister of the Naval Service:
Re Victoria Sealing Company.
Sir:-
I beg to acknowledge your letter of the 29th November, 1916. I observe you state that the award was made in the light of evidence submitted and that it has been decided to accept "the award of Mr. Justice Audette" as a final closing of the case. I desire respectfully to call attention to what may possibly have'been overlooked in this connection, namely: there has been no award. In this connection I refer to the Order in Council of the 10th June, 1913, which appointed Louis Arthur Audette, assistant judge of the Exchequer Court, "a Commissioner under Chapter 104 of the Revised Statutes of Canada for the purpose of investigating all such claims .	.	. and that as soon as
possible thereafter the said commissioner do report to the Minister of Marine and Fisheries his proceedings under said Commission together with the evidence and his opinion."
I also refer to the Commission which appoints Audette "to be our Commissioner to conduct such enquiry," and again: 'We do hereby require and direct you, our said Commissioner, to report to our Minister of Marine and Fisheries of Canada the result of your investigation together with the evidence taken before you, and any opinion you may eee fit to express thereon."
Counsel for the Crown on the opening of the Commission stated he had been "requested by the Dominion Government to represent the Government upon the discussion of these claims before the Commissioner." He added: "I may say at the outset that the Government does not recognize any legal obligation or technical liability"; and again he stated that as a representative of the Government together with those who represented the claimants he hoped they would be able to "give Tour Lordship something upon which to base your report and finally to enable the Government to satisfy the claims and compensate those who have been injured by these international enactments."
The Commissioner also on the same occasion said :	"I think we have gone beyond the
question of liability or rather of legal liability. We know there is no legal liability. My idea is to do what in equity and good conscience would suggest itself. You are more in the bounty and grace of the Crown here than anything else. But you must show some reason why you make a claim and you must have some reason which would appeal to any one on a question of justice and equity.
In matters of much smaller importance when Mr. Justice Audette is acting in the capacity of a judge, there is a provision for an appeal to a higher tribunal, and since in this case he was simply appointed to take the evidence for the information of the Government, and if he deemed fit, to express an opinion, the Victoria Sealing Company, Limited, ventures to press its claim that before the case is finally closed those interested may be permitted to show cause why' his opinion should not be adopted by the Government.
To this letter the deputy minister replied at a later date, and, quoting from the Order in Council, said:
In accordance with this, the Commissioner submitted his report and gave his opinion as to

the persons entitled to he paid compeiisation and the amount of such compensation. The Government, after consideration of his report and findings, approved of them by Order in Council of the 2Sth of February last, and since then those entitled to compensation have received it. As I previously informed you, it has been decided to accept the disposal of the claims that has been made as a final closing of the matter.
Later on, as a result of the intervention of Sir Charles Hibhert Tupper on the question, j;he Prime Minister wrote to Mr. Adams, the secretary-treasurer of the Victoria Sealing Company, on January 6, 1917:
In reply to your letter of the 22nd November last I beg to say that the report of Mr. Justice Audette and the petition for rehearing had been referred to the Hon. Arthur Meighen, Solicitor General, for report.
I have given the facts in the record as they come before me, and apparently the matter is in this position: that the Government have referred it to the Solicitor General for report. I am not here to criticise, and I do not widh to 'be understood as doing anything 'but putting before the House and the Government the case in regard to a very important international matter, and to ask the Government to take it into their very serious consideration, because it is a matter that has been the subject of consideration of three international tribunals. We had, first, the Paris tribunal of 1893; then we had the conference in Quebec in 1898, and then we had the final adjustment in 1911, all being based, so far as I can judge from those documents, upon the fact that the Victoria Sealing Company were, in the first instance, the major people in the industry; that they were paid compensation at one period on account of .the regulations interfering with them, and that at this later period they were unquestionably prevented from engaging in their business by reason of the regulations based upon the Paris award. Were it not for the fact that they weTe damaged by reason of the operation of those regulations, the Canadian Government would not have had a case to obtain a single dollar .from the American Government, with the exception of what they might have had for 'those four other isolated vessels which were fishing illegally. It is a curious way in which to dispose of an international trust, to provide for a payment of money to men who disregard the international agreement and fail to compensate those who 'observed the regulations to which the good faith of the country was pledged, who kept in touch with the Government of the day from time to time, and
who dealt with the situation, having regard to those principles upon which international matters should be dealt with.
I submit that the Government ought to * regard this question as still open, and take such course as they may deem fit. Once they recognize the existence is a valid claim they should assess what would be considered reasonable damages. The Victoria Sealing Company simply asks that the Government of Canada shall keep faith with them, and that the compensation agreed to in 1898 through Sir Louis Davies, again agreed to in 1909 with Earl Grey, and admitted to be their just due in 1913 by Mr. F. Curran, Crown counsel, before the Royal Commission, shall be paid to them by the Government of Canada as the funds .come in from time to time. The company only recently discovered after a long period of time that the Order in Council had been passed.
So the matter stands this way: The Canadian Government, having 'been entrusted by the Imperial Government for the first time in history with the conduct of negotiations involving a question of foreign policy and justice as between the Crown and its subjects, has exploited the injuries of British subjects to obtain on behalf of those subjects compensation amounting to $7,250,000, and having from time to time over a period of twenty years, by words and acts, given those subjects to understand that they would be fairly and equitably compensated, now turns round like a defaulting trustee and denies any part of that compensation to those on whose behalf they received it.
Had t'he reasons given in the report of the commissioner been contained in a judgment in a case between .subject and subject, there would have been a right of appeal where the grounds of the decision could have been reviewed. That appeal could only turn on the broad principles on which this matter aright to be determined, and not upon any narrow ground, not upon any technical provision of law.
It does seem to me that it would be a disgrace to Canada if, after our'dealings'on this question with the various nations interested, after utilizing this particular company as one institution which gave us the right to compensation, we should turn round and say to that company: We will pay you nothing because you cannot sue the Crown. The Government should proceed upon the broad principles laid down by Lord Chief Justice Coleridge and the

other justices in England in connection with the other treaty to which I have referred. The Government should act in a manner comporting with the dignity of the sources from which this money comes, and comporting with the dignity of the distinguished men who carried on these negotiations. I ask from the Government, who axe the custodians of this money, consideration of the request of this company, which I have endeavoured to present, not with any harshness or in any spirit of criticism, but simply as a case which I believe deserves the fairest possible consideration from the Government.
At six o'clock the House took recess.
After Recess.
