maintopic: CLAIMS UNDER PELAGIC SEALING TREATY.-VICTORIA, B.C. SEALING COMPANY.
speechtext:
At six o'clock the hon. member for Pictou (Mr. Macdonald) had just finished presenting to the House a question of some interest, a question which has been discussed here on one or two other occasions. He asked the Government for further consideration of the matter in so far as it conferred a compensation on certain parties to whom he thought compensation should be given. The minister concerned and his department gave very careful consideration to this whole subject, before Mr. Commissioner Audette was appointed to investigate the question and also after that appointment; and they have also given very careful attention to the findings of Mr. Justice Audette, and in those findings they concur. The Minister of Marine and Fisheries (Mr. Hazen) regrets not being here, and has asked me to deal with the matter in his absence. The hon. member for Pictou has argued that as a result of the Pelagic Sealing Treaty of 1911, a large sum of money will accrue to the treasury of this country, money which does not strictly belong to the people of the country generally, but which should be directed simply as a matter of compensation to those who have been engaged in the seal industry for many years prior to the treaty. He spoke particularly of the Victoria Sealing Company as being the parties chiefly interested. He has pointed out that they were not compensated, whereas the four or five other vessels which were, according to his assertion, sealing illegally at that time were compensated. In the first place, I can hardly agree with either of these contentions of my hon. friend. I do not wish to take up 
the time of the House in traversing the whole history of the matter, interesting as it is, but I want to touch on one or two points which, unless explained, might not be as clear to the House.
The United States acquired the Pribiloff islands as a part of Alaska, by purchase from Russia in 1867. Five years later she gave a lease for twenty years to the Alaska Commercial Company of the exclusive sealing rights on these islands. At that time and for some years afterwards there was no pelagic sealing of importance, so the lessees had a monopoly of the industry, resulting in very large profits to them, as well as to the lessors, the United States Government. In the early eighties some Canadians took up pelagic sealing in a more consistent way, and as good profits were made the industry soon grew. The lessee and the United States Government, seeing formidable competitors appearing, tried to stop them. The United States Government took the ground that Behring Sea is mare clausum and that as the seals were born and spent an important portion of each year on their islands, they were actually their property. In 1886, acting on the assumption that Behring Sea was a closed sea, they seized some Canadian sealing vessels in that sea many miles from land. The House will recall the diplomatic negotiations which followed at that time. No seizures were made the following year, but as pelagic sealing kept on growing, further seizures were effected in 1888 and in 1889. Vigorous diplomatic correspondence ensued, and in 1891 a modus vivendi was entered into, with a view to preventing further overt acts during negotiating, by which Behring Sea was closed to pelagic sealing and land killing was restricted to the number required to provide food for the natives on the islands, seal meat .forming an important portion of their food. This modus vivendi was continued in 1892. The negotiations finally resulted in an agreement to submit the whole question to arbitration, which arbitration took place in Paris in .1893. A condition of the arbitration was that the question of the natural history of the seal should be considered with a view to the proper protection of the herds. Canada's contentions were absolutely upheld. Pelagic sealing was vindicated as a legal method of hunting, and the United States was required to pay heavy damages for the seizures and interference made; but regulations for the protection of the seals, since known as the Paris award regulations were also

provided by the arbitrators. These regulations restricted the use of fire-arms to rifles outside of Behring Sea, and prohibited the use of fire-arms altogether in such sea, and also provided a close season for Behring Sea during the months of May, June and July.	_
During the first year the regulations were in operation there was a very large catch of seals, but every year subsequently the catch diminished very rapidly. It was obvious to everybody who studied the history of seal life that the regulations could only retard the extinction o'f the sealing industry, and it was very questionable whether they could permanently save it if pelagic sealing was followed. I need not go into the reasons except to mention that the killing of the seals on the rookeries enables the killers to select the male seals, whereas in the pelagic sealing there must be indiscriminate killing of the females as well as the males, and in the end the absolute extinction of the whole industry. As I have stated, the industry began to fail rapidly after 1894, and fell into such a bad way that British 'Columbia sealers got together and finally in 1900, formed what is known as the Victoria Sealing Company, because they realized that if all the sealing vessels which were then in existence went out in the indiscriminate loose way they were then going out, the whole business would be put an end to in a very short time. At that time there were 46 British Columbia sealing vessels, of which 43 were embraced in the Victoria 'Sealing Company. Year by year fewer vessels were sent out. In 1904 only 16 vessels were sent out by the company; in 1908, 4 vessels; in 1909, one vessel; and subsequently none. So that for two years before the treaty of 1911 was effected the Victoria Sealing Company had ceased to be a factor in the industry. While the Victoria Sealing Company dropped out of the business entirely after 1909, a few independent British Columbia boats continued in it.	[DOT]
Had it not been for the continuation of these few boats in the industry, carrying on active sealing operation, there practically would have been no reason for the United States entering into this treaty o' 1911, so far as Canada is concerned. It was therefore obvious that the best interests of all concerned wTould be served if an ar. rangement could be made by which the nonrookery-owning powers-the powers that had not an interest in the land operations of sealing-could fairly share in the business and have pelagic sealing done away with altogether. To this end, negotiations were taken up and resulted in the eminently satisfactory treaty which we are now discussing, of July 7, 1911, by which Canada receives 15 per cent of the gross number of skins taken on the United States and Russian sea islands, and 10 per cent of those taken on the shore islands, without incurring any expense as to the management of the herds. The treaty also provided for an advance payment of $200,000 on account of the skins which Canada would be entitled to under it, the object, no doubt, being to pay compensation to be paid under the treaty without drawing on the treasury. The treaty is for a terfn of 15 years, but it is expected that it will be continued indefinitely thereafter.
Following the adoption of the treaty, claims for compensation began to pour in, not only on account of it but also owing to the Paris award regulations, and for various other reasons. It was finally decided by the Government to appoint Mr. Justice Audette of the Exchequer Court a commissioner to investigate all claims flowing from or arising out of the pelagic sealing treaty of 1911, as also arising out of the Par's award regulations of 1894. His instructions will be found in the Order in Council passed appointing him. Some 1,605 claims amounting to over $9,000,000, were submitted to Mr. Justice Audette, and in order that the claims might 'be properly investigated without avoidable trouble or expense to the claimants, Judge Audette went to Victoria, British Columbia, and also to Halifax and Sydney and Ottawa, holding meetings at each place. Evidence under oath was submitted and counsel was employed by the Government to see that its interests were properly considered, as well as by the claimants with Tegard to the claims under the Paris award regulations, among which were those of the Victoria Sealing Company. The commissioner found they could not be paid, and he concluded his reasons ifor so finding in the following Words:
It Is conceded by all parties that the sealers have no legal claim. Their claims do not originate In tort, as in the case of the illegal seizure of the vessels under the British flag in 1886. This commission originated absolutely in the benevolence, grace and bounty of the Crown; and while I am not here holding the scale of justice on strict legal rights, but with rights emanating from equity and good conscience, I am unable to find that the sealers were in any manner injured and damaged by the regulations that would entitle them to compensation. It would be contrary to the prin-

ciples of natural justice to declare these claimants entitled to recover, where no pretence of right in law, equity or good conscience (ex aequo et borio) has been made out.
It has been contended that because the nation is recovering a large amount in consideration for the entering into the treaty of 1911, a monetary condition which would never have been obtained but for the regulations which kept the seals alive up to that time, that the sealers should recover. A most erroneous view to take under the circumstances. Whatever amount is recoverable-or recovered-under the treaty, forms a national fund absolutely at the disposal of the sovereign under constitutional principles, and which falls into the Canadian exchequer, and it is not even in any way earmarked to compensate the sealers under the treaty of 1911, and indeed, asserted with much more certitude not to compensate under the regulations which wdre made under the Paris Award in 1893 and which did not provide for the payment of any money but only sought thd protection of the herd.	_
If the Government were using moneys derived from the treaty of 1911, as claimed by some counsel, to pay the claimants under the regulations-moneys coming from two countries that had nothing to do with the regulations would thus be used. Hence it could not be done.
Having thus passed in review the general heads of complaint put forward by the sealers against the regulations, and approaching the consideration of this claim in a spirit of justice connoting the idea of doing what in equity and good conscience is fair and just, and after giving this branch of the commission special care and labour, as it involved both large amounts and a large number of claimants, I have come to the conclusion and find that the Canadian sealers are not entitled to be paid any compensation by the Crown for alleged damage resulting from the said regulations.
The commissioner found that the only persons entitled to compensation were those who were engaged in the industry in 1911, with certain minor exceptions, such as hunters who were prevented from hunting in that year, ow'ing to sickness or otherwise; also, the ships which were engaged in that year. The total amount of the compensation awarded was $60,663.75. The commissioner's report was approved, and these claims have been paid and it has been decided not to re-open the question. It is curious to note, as showing the arguments which appealed also to the Japanese Government, that in compensating their claimants they dealt only with those men who were actually engaged in the industry when the treaty came into eeffct in 1911. It is quite obvious that this large fund, which, we hope, will accrue .to the country from the preservation of these seal herds, belongs, not in particular to one person or another who may at one time or another have been engaged in the (sealing industry, hut belongs to the people of Canada in recognition of a right which they had to con-

duct pelagic sealing, and because that right has been extinguished or is abolished- has been given up by the whole people of Canada-therefore Canada is entitled to the compensation, and not those individuals who may have been engaged in the industry at one time but who, on account of regulations and conditions which were established to preserve the seal industry, and without which the industry would have become extinct, were compelled to abandon the industry. The Government therefore decided that the only people strictly entitled to any compensation are those who, at the time of the affirming of this treaty, were actually engaged in the business, and to whom, therefore, the contracting parties had to say: You cannot conduct sealing operations any longer.
With respect to the gentlemen of whom my hon. friend spoke to-day, it can only he again observed that they actually, by the conditions which existed at that time, had gone out of the business entirely two years prior to the contracting parties entering into that treaty. I can add nothing further than to say that this is the view taken by the minister and the department and the view generally taken by the Government. I cannot give my hon. friend any assurance that the Government would think it right, wise or advisable, after the whole matter has been thoroughly gone into by Mr. Justice Audette, a special commissioner who heard all evidence presented on behalf of the claimants and who had made a certain report, to appoint (another commission to investigate the work of Mr. Justice Audette. We feel that he dealt with it fairly and justly, and, on the whole, the Government feel that it must adhere to that report.

My- hon. friend ('Mr. Burrell) who has charge of this department in the absence of the Minister of Naval Affairs 'Concluded his observations by stating that he could not give any assurance that the Government would take into its favourable consideration the claim put forth this afternoon by the hon. member for Pictou (Mr. Macdonald') on behalf of the sealers of British Columbia. My hon. friend from Pictou did not expect any assurance to that effect to-day, but I still express the hope that the consideration of the Government will be more favourable in the future in regard to this question. It is impossible to deal fairly with this question, in my judgment, if we deal simply upon the strict letter of the Treaty of 1911. In order to do full

justice to the whole question on behalf of the people of Canada and of the sealers of British Columbia, I think it is imperative that we should go very much beyond the Treaty of 1893 which resulted in the passing of the regulations which are at the source of all the complaints we have now to deal with. Up to 1873 there was no such thing as pelagic sealing. As stated by my hon. friend, when the Pribyloff Islands belonged to Russia, and after their acquisition by the United States, the method of taking the seals was to kill them on the land. I am prepared to concede that perhaps this method was more conducive to the maintenance of the herd than any other. But my hon. friend will grant that the seal belongs to everybody, and not to one class of people in particular. In 1873, when some enterprising Canadians in British Columbia undertook to go into what was known as pelagic sealing-that is the hunting of the seals on the high seas-they were absolutely within their rights. This' industry became profitable. But the possessor of Pribyloff island, the American Government, and the lessees of the American Government, looked upon the pelagic sealers as intruders, interlopers and trespassers. T'he habits of these seals are peculiar. They live in the high seas in winter and resort to the land in May, June and July foT breeding purposes. When August comes they disperse again to the ocean and come back to the island the following spring. When they were dispersed on the ocean the British Columbia sealers pursued. In this, as I have said these sealeTS were perfectly within their right, and the only objection which was made was that pelagic sealing tended to deplete the herds. As stated by my hon. friend the objection was that the sealers who killed on the land destroyed only the young males, whereas on the high seas not only the young males but also the females were killed. But, as the pelagic sealers were absolutely within their rights, the protest of the American owners of the islands did not impress them. As has been stated by my hon. friend, in 188G the American authorities chose to seize several of the sealers. They claimed, as has been stated by my hon. friend from Pictou (Mr. Macdonald) and repeated by the hon. Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Burrell) that the Behring sea, where the seizures took place, belonged to the United States. This contention was rejected by the commission, and rightly so. I believe upon this point that the commission were unanimous. If I remember rightly the American counsel claimed that pelagic sealing ought to be altogether forbidden. The tribunal did not agree to this, but simply passed certain regulations to limit the pelagic sealing, and make it more difficult. These regulations were four in number. First, a close season- was established lasting, if I remember well, from May to August or September. There was a shoal oE sixty miles along Pribilof island where the seals breed. A zone was established around this shoal within which pelagic sealing w-as absolutely prohibited. Then, the use of certain weapons was prohibited; and, lastly, the use of -steam vessels was also forbidden. With these restrictions-the season, the zone, the weapon, and the vessels -the operation of the sealers was greatly limited, and undoubtedly they suffered damage. There cannot be a shadow of a doubt that they -suffered damage. They made complaints and representations to the Canadian Government. I may observe to my hon. friend that, if the award was unanimous as to the right of Canadians to engage in pelagic sealing, the award which established these regulations was not unanimous. Sir John Thompson, the appointee of the Canadian Government on the Board, did not agree to thi-s part of the award. The fact that a man of the eminent authority of Sir John Thompson would not -agree to these regulations is a very strong point on behalf of the sealers, and it is, to my mind, conclusive evidence that the -sealers had a just cause of complaint when these regulations were made. Therefore, it will be easily understood -why the sealers made complaint to the Canadian Government representing that they had been unfairly dealt with, and were entitled to compensation. That was in 1893. The matter was taken into consideration by the government of th-at day, but no conclusion was arrived at. In 1898, when the Joint High Commission was appointed to settle many questions that were then pending between Canada and the United States-the Atlantic Fisheries, the Alas-kan Boundary and others-this question of the seals was taken up by the Government. The Canadian representative brought the matter to the attention of his fellow-members of the commission, and claimed compensation for the British Columbian -sealers. It is to be observed that the fairness of this claim was not disputed by the American commissioner; on the contrary, it was accepted -as fair, and witnesses were examined by the commission to ascertain what would be the amount of compensation to which the Brit-

ish Columbia sealers might be fairly entitled. The matter, however, did not reach a conclusion, because the commission adjourned, and took up the consideration of the Alaskan boundary question, and the sealing question was never resumed. The matter stood where it was. The British Columbian sealers never ceased to make complaint to the Government, representing that they were entitled to compensation for the loss of their industry.
In 1909, when the Canadian Government was approached by the United States Government on the subject of the entire suspension of pelagic sealing, the Canadian Government agreed to the suspension of pelagic sealing for fifteen years, but only upon the condition that compensation should be given to Canada for the loss ol the right which she was sacrificing.
Was that in 1909?

Yes. The commission was appointed in 1910, if I remember rightly, and the final treaty was passed in July, 1911. It was stipulated as an absolute condition by the Canadian Government for the giving up of the privilege ol pelagic sealing that compensation should be afforded, and that condition was accepted by the United States authorities. Generous terms of compensation were granted; fifteen per cent of the value of the catch of seals killed on land, and an immediate advance of $200,000. What was the object of this compensation? My hon. friend says that it was a consideration for Canada's giving up her right to use the high seas for pelagic sealing. But Canada would not, for a sum of money, have given up such a right as that upon the high seas. The Canadian Government could not have been blind to the fact That people were engaged in that industry; that the industry had been seriously damaged year after year by the regulations which had for their object the restricting of pelagic sealing. It is not to be wondered at, therefore, that the Canadian Government could not ignore the claim of these men who had been engaged in pelagic sealing and whose rights had been so restricted. For my part, I always thought that the best way of investing this money would he to compensate the men who had suffered from these regulations. These men who built schooners and manned and equipped them for use in pelagic sealing were absolutely within their rights; they were absolutely as free as anybody else was on the high seas. Suddenly the Canadian Government said; You shall not carry on your trade any longer. The com-
missioner who was appointed, Mr. Justice Audette-a man of eminent ability, I admit; a man upon whose judgment I rely-

Before my hon. friend
leaves that point, may I ask him whether he has considered what would have happened if the sealing had been carried on after 1911 as it was from 1895 down to 1911? The evidence is that if there had been' no treaty, these people would have been put out of business by the absolute extinction of the seal herds.

The result of
these regulations was to make the business less profitable, and the sealers who had organized themselves into a corporation went less and less into the business. It is said that for three or four years before 1911 they had ceased to send schooners out on the high seas. But they never ceased to make application for compensation in respect of the damage that these restrictions had caused to them. If they went out of business, what was the reason? Simply that the regulations had made sealing unprofitable. That is to say, they suffered in consequence of the regulations imposed upon them.	'

That may be so, but if these regulations-which, after all, have had some effect in preserving the herds-had not been enforced, the sealers would have gone out of business sooner, because no seals would have been left.

Many industries which have flourished for a time in newly discovered districts have in the course of time exhausted .their material. The ore of many a mine has become or may yet become exhausted, and when exhausted no claim can be made from the state; but if while there is ore in th^ mine the miner is prohibited from working by the state, the latter receiving profits from the prohibition, the miner, out of the profits derived by the state, ought to receive compensation. So in this case. These men were exercising a right. Possibly in the course of time the sealing would have .been exhausted; I am very much afraid that a great deal of our wild animal life will be exhausted in the course of time. But so long as the trade is there, it can be taken hold of; and if the trade is suddenly cut on by legislative action, it seems to me there is just claim for compensation on the part of those whose rights are affected. I may be told that there is no legal claim; that the Government can

in this -case exercise its right of eminent domain. I admit that, but the sealers never had the pretension to claim from the Government any legal right in the matter. I put it simply on the ground of good conscience:	since the Canadian Government
has received several hundred thousand dollars, by way of compensation,' which are now in the public treasury, is it not right and fair that the men whose business has been destroyed hy the action of this Government, whatever its 'motive may have been, should foe compensated? It is not to the honour of 'Canada that the Government received this money from the American Government and has not compensated the men whose money has been put into the sealing industry. These men built something like seventy schooners, which have remained idle; the money which they put into their 'business has been absolutely lost. Yet they have received not a single dollar of compensation. Moreover, their schooners are useless for any other purpose than that for which they were designed and built. In view of the fact that the Government has received a large sum of-money in consequence of the very impediment which they have put in the way of these men, in fairness and equity the Government should compensate them -for the money they put into the (business. By action of the Government of Canada-with the purpose of which I am in sympathy-the business of these men was completely destroyed; therefore, out of the money received by the Canadian Government by way of compensation these men should foe the first to foe compensated.
I have read with care the judgment of Mr. Justice Audette. It seems to me that he takes a narrow view of this matter. He seems to have approached it more or less from the point of view of narrow justice, as it were, rather than from the point of view of, as he says, good conscience and equity. Well, every man may have his own opinion about what is equity, and justice, and good conscience. The application of a definite law dealing with a specific matter is one thing, fout in this case no question of law is involved.
It is altogether within the discretion of the men who are now in office to say whether those people shall be compensated or not. If it were a case of taking money out of the treasury for those people, I might say that the Government should not be asked to put their hands into the treasury in order to compensate them, but this is 378
money paid by the American Government for the destruction of those people's industry. There is absolutely no question on that point. Having received the money on that basis, equity and good conscience make it imperative that the money so received should go first to compensate the men whose business has been destroyed. Will this not appeal to the judgment of the gentlemen who are on the treasury benches? Up to the present time, they have refused to depart from the opinion expressed by Mr. Justice Audette. My only objection to his opinion is that he takes too narrow a view. This is a matter which is of no personal concern to any one of us. I do not know who the claimants are. I saw Captain Adams only once in my life. I was, however, in office when this treaty was negotiated. I gave the matter my best consideration, and I thought then that when we received money as compensation, the first men to be paid out of that money ought to be those whose business and livelihood had been destroyed, and whose good money had become worthless. For these considerations, I hope, although my hon. friend will refuse to give an assurance that those men will foe more equitably dealt with than in the past or that their claims will be considered, that the Government will reconsider their attitude upon this matter, and see that after all, if we are to treat this matter in equity and good conscience, we should give those men the money.

speakeroldname: Mr. D. D. McKENZIE (North Cape Breton) :
speechtext:
Mt. Speaker, were it not for the fact that a great many people from the county which I have the honour to represent here were interested directly in this industry which is now under discussion, I would not venture to add a word to what has been so ably presented to the House by the leader of the Opposition and the hon. member for Pietou, and replied to by the Minister of Agriculture. As early as the year 1887, several vessels from the Atlantic coast went around Cape Horn and engaged in this	business on the	British	Columbia	coast. Ever since	then,	until theindustry was closed out by international regulations and regulations of this Government, the owners of those vessels kept in touch with that industry. Amongst those men were Captain Charles Haekett, Captain J. W. Peppett, Captain Cutler, Captain	Ryan, Captain	Frank	Haekett,Captain Desmond, Captain	Bissett
and Captain LeBlanc. Some of them were absolute owners of the vessels, and all of



them were interested in the business which they followed. From 1887 down to 1893, and since then down to 1911, at the consummation of the treaty mentioned by several hon. gentlemen here to-day, they conducted a profitable business in the sealing industry with their headquarters in British Columbia. As has already been fully explained, for international reasons and for the purpose of conserving this very valuable industry, and conserving the lives of those seals, it wias thought proper to enter into negotiations, and an agreement was made by which that industry was closed out. Those men had a vested interest and a vested right in that industry, just the same as the Minister of Agriculture has a vested right in a certain industry in British Columbia. And I presume that if those who are engaged in the fruit industry of British Columbia were, for some reason, prevented from engaging in that industry, he would ably advocate their rights. I think he would say that if those who have put their money into orchards, or mines, or fisheries in British Columbia were, for some international reason, cut off from their employment, and if moneys were paid into the treasury of Canada as a compensation and consideration for the closing down of those industries, those who were in those businesses and whose occupations were so cut off should be the first to be considered in the division of that money. The interpretation given to that treaty by the leader of the Opposition should receive due consideration. If a certain document is in writing or if a certain statute goes through Parliament, the man who wrote the document or who drafted the Act or had a hand in putting it through Parliament, has perhaps no more to say as to the proper interpretation of it than anybody else, because a judicial interpretation must be given as to the meaning the words in it must bear. But when international negotiations are conducted, as the negotiations in regard ' to this treaty were conducted, and when all the motives and ideas are not put into writing, the views of the then Prime Minister of the country, who was one of the parties to those negotiations, and who knew what the negotiations were, should be considered when the matter is discussed. We are told by the right hon. gentleman who leads the Opposition, but who was the Prime Minister of this country at the time this treaty was negotiated and received the approval of His Majesty and passed into an international bargain, that the intention was that, so far as that agreement cur-fMr. McKenzie.]
tailed the profits of any people engaged in the sealing industry, they should be compensated as far as the money received would go. That is the interpretation given to the treaty by the man who negotiated it._ That being the case, that being the idea conveyed to those people by the Government of the day and by the Prime Minister who negotiated the agreement, it is incumbent upon those who succeeded him in office to carry out that policy. The Government may eay: If we had been in power at the time, we would not have made such an agreement; we would not have stopped the industry, we would not have interfered with the people who were working in it, and if we had interfered with them at all, we would not have paid them any compensation. But the King and the power of the King were represented at that time by the Prime Minister of that day, and he made a certain arrangement. It is, therefore, incumbent upon the Government of the day to carry it out. This principle has been recognized in this country before. Hon. gentlemen in this House, and particularly hon. members of the Government, remember the treaty of Washington, in connection with which there was what is well known as the Fisheries Award. There was paid into the treasury of Canada on account of the award the sum of $5,000,000. The Government of the day did not think that was money that they could apply in the ordinary way; they considered it was something that belonged practically to the fishing industry of this country. What happened-and what is the law to-day-was that at least a certain amount of that money was placed at interest, and the interest of it is paid as a bounty to the fishermen of Canada. Everyone knows that the fishermen of Canada on both coasts receive a bounty. That money comes to them out of this Washington treaty fisheries award. Because the treaty of Washington permitted a condition of things that meant interference to some extent with the fishery business, the money that came to the Government by reason of the concession given to American fishermen was divided amongst the fishermen of Canada, and is being divided in that way to-day. The taking of this money which we get for the sealing industry and establishing some equitable basis upon which it will be divided amongst those people whose interests are affected by reason of the treaty, would be only carrying out, and perhaps extending to a certain degree, the principles that were estab-

lished by the Government of the day in connection with the award paid to this country under the treaty of Washington.
I submit, therefore, that it would not be doing anything new if the Government took this money and made such an equitable division of iit between the corporations and the men who were engaged in this business on the basis of the facts as they were ascertained.
As I understand the findings of Mr. Justice Audette, they do not go the full length ot the principle involved in this quest'on. I understand his position to be that no person has any claim on the Government for any part of this money, and. that no person could at law establish a claim against the Crown for it. I need not tell you, Sir, or any member of the Government that you cannot establish a claim against the Crown except by statute; that is, unless there is an Act of Parliament fixing that obligation upon the Crown. Mr. Justice Audette could have made a finding of that sort at the start. The moment he discovered there was no such statute he could have said that it was useless to go any further. But that was not the idea of starting the investigation, and perhaps I am doing him an injustice in saying that that was his conclusion, but, nevertheless, as I understand it, that was his conclusion.
The Government, as representing the Crown, are mere trustees of this money. They receive the money in trust for a certain specific purpose, and it is their duty to divide it properly and equitably upon the basis of the facte as they appear. In the colony of Newfoundland and in the provinces of New Brunswick, Prince Edward Island, and Nova Scotia, and particularly that part of Nova Scotia to which I belong, there were hundreds of people engaged in this industry. Many vessels were bought on the Atlantic coast, taken around the Horn and engaged in the sealing business on the other side. But all these people were put out of business 'by the treaty. I submit that when there is in the hands of the Government money that was paid to them under a treaty that put an end to this industry, the people who were engaged in it have a claim in equity, and justice, and good conscience against the Government. I submit that if it is found that Mr. Justice Audette's decision is not wide enough, or that he has not gone sufficiently deep into this question, further investigation should be made, and a further opportunity to be heard should be given to the people whose interests are

affected. If the Government should find that they are mere trustees for this money, and that it was to be given to the people who were engaged in this industry, I trust they will not permit any mere technicalities to stand in the way, but will deal with the matter broadly and properly as the justice of the case demands.

speakeroldname: Hon. O. J. DOHERTY (Minister of Justice) :
speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
It appears to be common ground
that there is no question involved here of a legal right on the part, of those whose cause has been pleaded here this afternoon. The question is one entirely of what ought to be done in equity and good conscience, and the question was so submitted to Mr. Justice Audettte, and so dealt with by him. The contention of hon. gentlemen who have spoken in support of 9 p.m. some further recognition of this claim seems to me to rest, if I may say ,so with all respect, upon a misapprehension of what it was that this money was paid for. Their reasoning would lead one to believe that they look upon it as money paid for damage suffered in the past. Now a glance at the treaty of 1911 will show that what was paid for was the foregoing by Canada, on behalf of her citizens, of the right to carry on pelagic sealing for a period of time in the future. The loss, therefore, that was, being compensated for was a loss that might occur to people in the future.

Here was the Victoria Sealing Company with its vessels all prepared, but they were unable to carry on their business by reason of these regulations. The minister must not forget that the basis of our contention in the negotiations with the American Government was the fact that in, the past there were deprivations of that character.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
I was coming to the
position, as I understand it, of the Victoria Sealing Company, but I think it is well to get clear at the outset what this money was paid to us for-because until we know what it was paid to us for, it is impossible for us to ascertain who has any particular or specific claim upon that money as distinct from the claim of the whole public of Canada, [DOT] for whom the Government received' and holds this money. What was paid for, was the foregoing for fifteen years, then in the future, of the privilege on the part of Canada, as representing all Canadians, of exercising the right of pelagic sealing. Now that right of pelagic scaling that we agreed to forego for that period of time in the

future was the right to pelagic sealing as that right could legally be exercised at the time the treaty was entered into; that is to say, the right to pelagic sealing subject to the regulations of the Treaty of Paris. That right had been 60 limited and so restricted by the regulations of the Treaty of Paris that this Victoria Sealing Company in particular h.ad, as I understand the facts, abandoned the business.

No,	the Victoria
Sealing Company never abandoned the business.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Ceased to carry on the business.

By reason of the
fact that the regulations of the Treaty of Paris prevented them from doing so.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
That	is precisely
what I am pointing out. The regulations of the Treaty of Paris made it not worth while for the Victoria Sealing Company to carry on the 'business, and that was the condition when the treaty was entered into whereby Canada, on behalf of her people, renounced the Tight of carrying on the business under the treaty which is now in question, and received compensation for her renunciation of the right to carry on the business under those conditions. That right to carry on the business was open to every Canadian citizen just as fully as it was to the Victoria Sealing Company, and the compensation was to Canada as a whole for foregoing something in the future.

Not necessarily, it was not so stated.
Mr. DOHERTY": That is the treaty. What did we do? We agreed to forego the right to pelagic sealing for fifteen years to come, and for that -we were to (be paid this proportion of the catch that was to be got in those fifteen years to come.
Not in the fifteen years to come, because there was no right to make it.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: We agreed to forego the right. Our people had the right to carry on the pelagic sealing, subject to the regulations of the Treaty of Paris.

No, my hon. friend is not correct in that, because, if he will permit me, the conclusions of the Treaty of Paris say that we could carry that on in the open sea, but it was of no value, seeing that we could not Teach the rookery.
[ Mr. Doherty.]

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: This is all a question of pelagic sealing. If that was of no value at all, it cannot have been of any value to the Victoria Sealing Company any more than to anybody else. Whatever its value was, much or little, that is what we had in 1911, and that was the only thing we could forego, because we could not forego what we had not. The United States Government undertook to pay this compensation to this country, as the representative of all its inhabitants, for our renunciation of the exercise of that right, whatever may have been its value, for a period of time to come. That right, as it stood at that time, the thing that we agreed to forego, was a right which in the judgment of the Victoria Sealing Company was not worth while .for it to exercise, and it had ceased to exercise that right. The Victoria Sealing Company therefore stood in the same position as any other citizen of Canada who did not find that under the conditions it was worth while to carry on that business. When we come to deal with consideration of individuals, we have to remember that the money we have is not the price of anything that happened in the past. It is the price of our foregoing a right for the future, and whoever would be affeoted fairly and equitably in the future by that remuneration of ours, ought to get compensation, and fairly enough those who were actually exercising this right at the time we agreed to forego it, have been considered and have been compensated. The refusal is as regards the people who, three or four years before, made up their minds it was not worth their while to exercise the right-
No.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: -demonstrating therefore that they would not be among the class of people affected by the fact that we renounced that right for the next fifteen years.
In the argument my hon. friend is making, he is excluding altogether the fact that this company kept its ships tied up by the wharf on account of the understanding with the Government.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
With all respect, I think my hon. friend is quite mistaken when he says that those people who sent their ships out did so in violation of the regulations of the Treaty of Paris. I think the best demonstration of the fact that they did not violate the treaty is that they were able to carry on operations with impunity, and were never seized. They went out in the
- SEPTEMBER 18, 1917
*exercise of the rights of pelagic sealing, subject to the regulations of the Treaty of Paris, and they thought it worth their while. They are, therefore, among the class of people who, presumably at all events, would ' have gone on if this last treaty had not been passed, and they are the people who in a particular manner, different from all other citizens of Canada, are affected by our renunciation of that right. They are fairly and equitably the people who ought to be compensated, and they are the people who were compensated. But to carry the argument made on behalf of the Victoria Sealing Company to its logical conclusion, if that company is entitled to remuneration on the grounds stated, then it seems to me that anybody who at any time had carried on the business of pelagic sealing, ought to get compensation, because that ground is that though they had ceased to carry on the business, and though it clearly appeared that they were not going to carry it on in any way during the fifteen years covered by the treaty they had at some past time carried on the business of pelagic sealing. That was the matter that was submitted to Mr. Justice Audette. I think that there can be no claim upon those moneys on the part of those people as being deprived of something they otherwise would have had in the future is most clearly established by the fact that when it is sought to support their claim-and I refer particularly to the very interesting and very forcible speech of the right hon. leader of the Opposition (Sir Wilfrid Laurier)-it all has to be made to rest upon the damage it is claimed they sustained by reason of the regulations under the Treaty of Paris. Well, those regulations were passed and were in force for a number of years before this treaty, and those regulations were made by competent authority to control the carrying on of that business, and the loss that resulted to the Victoria Sealing Company or anybody else from the enactment of those regulations-
There was nobody else so far as Canada was concerned.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: My hon. friend from North Sydney (Mr. McKenzie) has just been telling us of a large number of people in his part of the country who were engaged in pelagic sealing.
They were in the Victoria Sealing Company.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: being utilized to compensate people who, in the conditions created hy t'he treaty, existing subsequently to the treaty, are carrying on their business at a disadvantage. They are people particularly affected hy the result of the treaty in a different way from every other individual Canadian . But here we are asked to apply that money not to indemnify anybody affected by the consequent effects of the treaty but somebody that-suffered a damage by reason of something that was done years before.

Is that not merely a
question of degree? In the fishery case they were at a disadvantage but were permitted to go on; but in the other case they were stopped altogether.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Being permitted to go on they are a class of people directly and particularly affected by the continued operation of that treaty, and therefore, if we get compensation for foregoing on behalf of the people of Canada the right under that treaty to carry on certain fishing operations, I can see the fairness and equity of applying some of that money to compensate people who, by reason of that treaty, are hampered in the industry they carry on. I am not contending that people who were carrying on the industry, at the time of this last treaty and were cut off from doing it should not have compensation to the extent of the damage they proved, and they have had it. I was just pointing out that the case we now are dealing with differs in every respect from the case of the fishermen to whom my hon. friend from North Sydney refers. I quite appreciate the sympathy of hon. gentlemen with these gentlemen who are interested in the sealing industry, but I must confess that, eliminating the question of legal obligation, trying to judge it as a question of what is fair and reasonable, I do not see that the Government of Canada, which has received this money in trust, just as all the moneys of Canada are in its hands in trust for all the people of Canada,-
Oh no, this is a special trust.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
That is precisely where I join issue. It is in trust for all the people who, during those fifteen years are deprived of this privilege, and I am prepared to concede that in equity and fairness, if there is any individual Canadian who shows that by Canada's renunciation of that right for that fifteen years he suffers a damage or an injury distinct and differ-

ent from that which is suffered by the wjaole public, he ought to get compensation.

What better case
could my hon. friend have in considering the matter of damage than that of a company which has tied up at the wharf six schooners especially built for the sealing industry and which is unable to use those schooners under the Paris regulations, and has not used them for fifteen years?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
They were unable, under the Paris regulations, to use them and that was their settled and defined position; and this treaty did not make them any more unable to use them, it left them precisely where they were in that regard. We are asked to compensate a man for being prevented under this treaty from carrying on a business that, in the conditions that existed before this treaty, he was unable to carry on.
What I have sought to make clear is that the damage to these people, in so far as they were damaged, resulted from what had taken place years before this treaty, and that this treaty left them neither better nor worse off; and this money was paid to us for the foregoing of a right, subsequent to the execution of the treaty that these people, by their own admission, were not in a position, by reason of anterior events, to exercise or avail themselves of.

How could it be possible by the law of Canada settled under this international agreement, for anybody to set up a claim during the fifteen years for the right to legally go out and seal in Behring sea and assert that they had vessels or schooners or anything of that kind, when it was well understood, it was known as a matter of public law, that it was impossible for anybody to go sealing?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: They were all subject to the regulations. The right that they had was to go out and fish subject to the regulations. On their behalf and on behalf of all the people of Canada, Canada renounced that right, and anybody deprived of the right which he was exercising to fish under the regulations was entitled to compensation. All of those who went so far towards showing that as to show that they were carrying on the business under the regulations, got compensation.
Where is the rest of it going?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
The rest of it belongs to Canada in the right of the whole of the

people of Canada. None of us can go pelagic sealing.
If the regulations under the treaty of Paris put an end to pelagic sealing, what had we to give up by this treaty of 1911?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
It did not put an end
to pelagic .sealing, it regulated and restricted pelagic sealing. If they had put an end to pelagic sealing then we would have had nothing to give up, just as the hon. gentleman says: It is not quite conceivable that if we had had nothing to give up, our American friends would have undertaken to pay us something approximating $7,000,000 for that nothing. We had something to give up, and there were people carrying oh pelagic sealing subject to the restrictions and regulations, and that is the right we had.
-Mr. MACDONALD:- Only four. What does the minister say to the consideration of this matter given by Mr. Found in this report to the Naval Department?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I have heard the reading of that report, and it would seem to indicate that Mr. Found was under the impression that something ought to be paid to these gentlemen. I hav-e difficulty in accepting that conclusion, although I have not carefully read the report. I have Tead with considerable care the report of Mr. Justice Audette, and I may add that before the matter wae submitted to the commission I had occasion to go with some degree of care into the consideration of this question, and for what value that may have, I may say that the conclusion of Mt. Audette was by no means a surprise to me. The impression I had formed was that that wae the only conclusion that could properly and fairly be reached.

Does the hon. gentleman think that, from the standpoint o-f equity, justice and fair play, a company with whom the Canadian Government was negotiating right along, with whom the Government had conferences immediately preceding the -treaty of 1911 as to the question o-f compensation, a company who had vessels prepared to go sailing, which were tied up to the wharf at Victoria, would have no bona fide reasonable claim* for consideration upon the Government of the day, and for some allowance out of this fund which is paid to tho-se who are to be prevented from sealing, realizing that nobody else would, in all human probability, prepare facilities for the purpose of engaging
in sealing during the next fifteen years, that are to come during part of which time sealing is prohibited?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
'We look at the matter from different angles. I do not think it would be equity, justice and fair play to the people of Canada in general if we took their money and gave it to some one for whom we were sorry because some years before-
Mr. -MACDONALD: What interest has the man in the interior in sealing?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: None special to himself. But here is $7,000,000 belonging to Canada, which the man in Ontario has -a share in, just the same as the man in British Columbia, and the only reason put forward so far I can see for paying -the money to these paaiti-cular individuals is -that, unfortunately for them, they invested money in an enterprise which, by regulation of competent authority, was made unprofitable. That seems to me to be the situation, and we are asked to take the money of the people of Canada and pay to these people for foregoing the right to carry on pelagic sealing under unprofitable conditions not by reason of this treaty, buit of the position created by previous regulations. We are asked to take the money- of the whole of the people of Canada and pay it to these gentlemen because we are sorry for them.

The whole question is a relative one. You can well understand that a man in British Columbia would not engage in sealing in Nova Scotia, or a man who was interested in the cultivation o-f soil in the prairies, who knew nothing about seas, would not engage in sealing in other parts o-f the Dominion. But if you have a case where the people have the vessels which are actually engaged in the enterprise tied up to the wharf, prepared to go out, hut prevented from going out by reason of regulations made by this Government with a foreign government, does the hon. gentleman mean to say that the owners of the vessels in close proximity to the place where the sealing can be carried on have no equity by which, they would be given the fir-st right to participate in the fund? The Government having agreed to a fifteen-yeai; prevention of sealing, nobody else in Canada would ever engage in it in that period.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I have tried to say what I mean to say.
I know -what the hon. gentleman has to say, but he has not met my point exactly.

I wish to call attention oi the House very shortly to a matter of which I gave notice to the Prime Minister (Sir Robert Borden) and to the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Burrell) yesterday, regarding the duty on potatoes. Some two or three weeks ago I asked the Government if ' it was their intention to make potatoes free under the provision of the United States Tariff Bill and under the War Measures Act.
I was promised consideration, and as nothing was said about it, on Thursday last I asked the Government the question. That question and the statement respecting it made on behalf of the Government are as follows:
Mr. F. B. Carvell (Carleton, N.B.) :	A week
or so ago I asked the Government if they would not consider the advisability of removing the duty on potatoes, the effect of which would be that our potatoes would have the right to enter the United States free of duty. I was promised consideration of the matter and I would now ask the minister if he is able to give an answer.
Sir Thomas White:	The matter referred to
by my hon. friend (Mr. Carvell) is one relating to the tariff. Announcements of that kind are not discussed in advance for reasons which will be obvious to the House. I am unable to make any statement with respect to the matter except to say that any action the Government may take will be announced in due course. It is impossible for me to make a statement in reference to the matter at the present time.
While the Minister of Finance (Sir Thomas White) is usually very courteous,
I thought he was rather testy about the matter, and I was rather surprised at the attitude he assumed. Therefore, I thought it in the interest of my constituents that I should give this matter some little publicity before prorogation. I do not intend to move an amendment, because I realize that such a motion on going to Supply would be treated as a vote of want of confidence, and this is a matter
of such great importance to my constituents that I am not going to offer an amendment and have it voted down. On the other hand. I want to present the case to the Government, and see if they will not act and do justice to the great body of people in the Maritime Provinces especially, and people all ever central Canada as a whole. I do not know that it is necessary to state that the cultivation of the potato is by far the greatest agricultural industry in. the Maritime Provinces. In the last two years the value of this crop in the Maritime Provinces has far exceeded any other agricultural product, and I think I should be safe in saying, all other agricultural products put together, though possibly this last statement may be a little extreme. In my own constituency last year according to the best of figures I could obtain, they received something like seven or eight million dollars for the potatoes which they disposed of. In that item I include the counties of Victoria and Carleton, because that is the constituency, a part of which at least I now represent. These two counties are by far the greatest potato-producting counties in Canada. But all the other counties along the St. John river, and to a very great extent on what we call the North Shore, and around the county of Westmorland, are great potato producing counties. In addition, there is the province of Prince Edward Island, where, if they had proper transportation facilities, the crop would far exceed that of any other portion of Canada, and I believe, of the North American continent. The House will see, from my cursory statement, that the potato industry in the Maritime Provinces is an important one, and any legislation affecting the production or price of potatoes is a matter of prime importance to the people of that portion of Canada. To give you some idea of the importance of this industry, I shall tead to the House a statement which I received to-day from the Commissioner of Customs:

I have tried to get the data, but have failed; I am giving the House the information that I have. A very large percentage of this business must have come from the Maritime Provinces and eastern Quebec. No portion of Canada has made such tremendous strides in the production of potatoes as the province of Quebec from Levis eastward, and, to some extent, westward. It is wonderful what the people of Quebec are doing, especially on the southern bank of the St. Lawrence river from Levis all the way to the Gaspe peninsula.
We know that practically all the potatoes that are imported into Canada come in the early summer, before our potatoes are available. So.that the duty of $200,000 that we pay on potatoes imported into Canada is paid at a time when we are compelled to import new potatoes because none of our own are available.
When you consider that those are the prices of the exporting country, and add to

that the cost of transportation and the cost of two or three profits, you will find that, by the time you get the potatoes to the consumer, instead of the cost of those potatoes being increased by $200,000, the increase as a result of that duty will be nearer $400,000. Those early potatoes are consumed very largely by people who are able to buy and pay for them, so that the increased price of them does not impose a hardship upon the ordinary labouring man that would be imposed by increased prices of many other articles through increased duties. It, however, greatly increases the cost of living in Canada under present conditions.	[DOT]
I wish to direct the attention of the House particularly to the question of the export of potatoes. In New Brunswick our farmers are raising, not a few hundred bushels but thousands of barrels. Many farmers in my constituency last year raised from 1,000 to 3,000 and 4,000 barrels each -we reckon our potatoes altogether by barrels instead of by bushels. Therefore, when you add a small amount of ten cents, or fifteen cents, or twenty cents a bushel, you have made a wonderful change in the income of the farmer. The duty on potatoes going into the United States is ten per cent ad valorem. If potatoes are worth $2 per barrel, as they are in New Brunswick today, and we send them over to the United States, if everything went properly, we would pay twenty cents a barrel for the purpose of getting those potatoes into the United States; or in other words, the farmer would get twenty cents a barrel more than he can possibly receive under present conditions. That is the way in which it works out. I am not going to argue now whether the importer or the exporter pays the duty, because that very largely depends upon the special conditions existing regarding each particular transaction, but so far as we in the Maritime Provinces are concerned, there is not any question about the matter-the Canadian farmer pays the duty. I live within ten miles of the boundary line and our farmers live up and down along that line, and potatoes are being raised on both sides of it. In Aroostook you will find that potatoes are worth the value of potatoes on our side of the line plus the duty. There i's no use in making any argument about the matter; those are the facts. A man can argue as mucn as he chooses, but those who go into the Maritime Provinces and get to know what they are speaking about would not listen to him.

speechtext:
Our potatoes in New Brunswick-go practically altogether to New England points, and they go almost wholly by rail. Potatoes from Nova Scotia and Prince Edward Island are carried by water to a great extent. In Nova Scotia, a limited trade has been carried on for many years, but that with the West Indian islands trade is only a bagatelle as compared with the trade with the United States. We hav.>, however, a big trade with Cuba, and that goes partly by water and partly by rail.
I am satisfied, if you investigate the details of the returns, you will find that a great proportion of the potatoes sent to Cuba last year, which came from my constituency and along the river St. John, were shipped by rail to Boston and from Boston to Cuba by water. That is the ordinary route of travel. I have one client and constituent who last year, to my knowledge, sold considerably over $100,009 worth of potatoes to Cuba alone and they all went by rail to Boston and thence by steamer. I have another client ^id constituent who must have handled $50,000 worth of potatoes in the same market, and from my knowledge, I believe a large pro-[DOT] portion of those potatoes came from New Brunswick. I find that during the fiscal year ended March 31, 1917, and the first five months of this year, we have sent to the United States about $3,800,000 worth of potatoes upon which we have paid a duty of 10 per cent, or $380,000. We have simply contributed that amount of monev to the revenues of the United States. In addition to that, we have sent to Cuba over $1,500,000 worth of potatoes, practically all of which went through American ports. If the duty were removed from potatoes going into the United States, we would save the duty on that portion as well, because the United States have a preferential treaty with Cuba-that is, potatoes from the United States can be sent into Cuba at a lower rate of duty than potatoes coming from any other part of the continent. If potatoes werd made free into the United States, of course our potatoes would all go to the United States and none of them direct to Cuba, they would be exported to the United States and then when they were properly in that country they could he sold to Cuba or wherever the buyers chose to send them. The result would 'he that all the potatoes going to Cuiba, as well as to the United States, would go free of duty, and that

would mean, on -the figures I have given, about $500,000 of extra money in the pockets of the people of New Brunswick.

and the first five months of this year. Prior to 1916 very few of these were sent to the United States, because after the passing of the Underwood tariff, under which potatoes were practically free-there was only a ten per cent ad valorem duty-certain very shrewd Yankees who live about forty or fifty miles from my home conceived the idea of throwing mud at the Canadian potatoes by claiming that they were afflicted with a disease known as powdery scab. It was all a myth; there never .was any powdery scab, but just the ordinary scab that we have seen on potatoes ever since we were
children. But these gentlemen scared their Government and our Government and everybody else, and I think I am safe in saying that it cost this Government almost $100,000 to fight the disease. Regulations and a rigid inspection were put in force and it was almost imposible for us to ship our potatoes across the line. But last year, when the United States wanted our potatoes, they did 'not bother very much about powdery scab or about regulations ana inspection. They wanted our potatoes' and were glad to get them. So last year would be the first in a great many years when trade flowed freely without any unnatural barriers. I admit that the valuation is very, very far in excess of what the same volume of business would amount to in an ordinary year.

2,800,000	bushels, and to Cuba 1,500,000 bushels. Altogether we exported practically

The United States customs authorities fix an arbitrary figure in arriving at the valuation. As I understand it, they do not take the invoice price of each carload of potatoes, but place an arbitrary figure upon potatoes from a certain area. At the present time that arbitrary figure for the Maritime Provinces is $3 a barrel, Actually our farmers are only getting $2 a barrel. The result is that under their method of assessing the duty is increased by fifty per cent,. With that exception, .trade is flowing as ,it naturally would under ordinary conditions.

I do not know. I only happen to know this because a few days ago

I received a letter from an organization in New Brunswick, known as the New Brunswick Potato Exchange, who are really the greatest potato dealers in Canada, pointing this out to me, and wanting to 10 p.m. know if something could not be done to remedy it. The result of this method of determining the duty by the United States is that we pay a great deal more than we really should. *
I would not attempt to say what the surplus in the United States will be this year, but I know it will be very large. As regards Canada, I have been told by gentlemen interested in the business that, without taking the Maritime Provinces at all, the surplus in Canada will be six or seven million bushels. If that toe true, it is perfectly safe to say that we shall have a surplus in Canada of at least 10,000,000 bushels, because in the maritime province alone I think we shall have a surplus of about
5.000.	000 or 6,000,000 'bushels. So if I am right in the information I have received- and if I am not the minister can correct me-the surplus this year will be easily
10.000.	000 bushels. In other years, when there has been a shortage of potatoes in Quebec and Ontario, we have been able to ship out potatoes there, tout when there is no shortage in Quebec and Ontario, we have no market for- our potatoes except the United States. Let me give the House an illustration of what that means. In the spring of 1915, there were, I think I am safe in saying, from half a million to a million bushels of potatoes sold in New Brunswick at 15 cents a bushel, and tens of thousands of bushels were thrown on the dump because there was not stock enough to eat them up. The reason for this condition was that there was no demand for potatoes in Quebec and Ontario, and we were debarred by the regulations from sending our potatoes to the United States. The House can readily see the importance of having the United States -market open to us. If the provinces of Quebec and Ontario want potatoes, we have them for them, but if they do not want them, unless we can sell to the United States or Cuba, we have absolutely no market and are in exactly the same position we were in in the spring of 1915.
